title: Explore Hospital Imaging Data
text:
These interactive charts use the CMS reporting period July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025. Each record is a hospital’s reported percentage for one measure. Select or hide measures in the legend, and hover over marks for details.


Each bar counts hospitals whose reported percentage falls in that score range. The measures are overlaid for comparison; use the menu to view either measure alone.









Bars show the median reported percentage among hospitals with an available score in each state or territory. A median summarizes a group; it is not a hospital rating, and differences can reflect many factors beyond care quality.

title: Explore Hospital Imaging Data
text:
Measure guide

OP-10 — Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material: The reported percentage of outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast.
OP-39 — Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates: The reported percentage of screening mammograms followed by diagnostic imaging within 45 days.

The measures describe different processes and should not be read as a single score of hospital quality. The CMS dataset provides hospital-level reported percentages; it does not explain why a particular hospital’s value differs.

title: About
text:
Data source
The analysis uses the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Outpatient Imaging Efficiency – Hospital dataset (dataset ID: wkfw-kthe). It contains hospital-level reported percentages for measures including abdomen CT use of contrast (OP-10) and breast cancer screening recall rates (OP-39), along with facility location and reporting-period fields. The charts describe these reported measures; they do not establish why hospitals differ or provide a complete assessment of care quality.
For field definitions, see the CMS hospital data dictionary (PDF).

title: Outpatient Medical Imaging Quality Across U.S. Hospitals
text:
For my final data science project, I am analyzing the Outpatient Imaging Efficiency - Hospital dataset published by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). This dataset tracks how hospitals across the United States use outpatient medical imaging tests, such as CT scans and mammography screenings, to evaluate efficiency and patient safety in diagnostic care.
In this project, I plan to explore key variables including hospital locations (states, cities, and ZIP codes), specific imaging measures (Measure ID and Measure Name), hospital efficiency Score values, and reporting dates (Start Date and End Date). By examining these variables together, I aim to compare medical imaging quality across different hospitals and states to see where outpatient imaging is used most effectively.
I chose this topic because I plan to become an ultrasound technician and want to learn more about medical imaging in healthcare. Understanding how imaging efficiency and recall rates are measured across facilities will give me valuable perspective on quality standards and patient care in diagnostic imaging.

title: Outpatient Medical Imaging Quality Across U.S. Hospitals
section: Distribution of Outpatient Imaging Measure Percentages
text:
Distribution of Outpatient Imaging Measure Percentages









This graphic compares the distribution of reported hospital percentages between July 2024 and June 2025 for the two measures in the CMS dataset: OP-10 (Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material) across 3,904 hospitals and OP-39 (Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates) across 3,247 hospitals. OP-10 represents the percentage of outpatient abdominal CT scans performed both with and without contrast material; in this dataset, half of reporting hospitals fall between 3.0% and 7.6% (median 5.0%), with a right-skewed tail reaching 61.7%. OP-39 represents the percentage of patients recalled within 45 days after a screening mammogram or digital breast tomosynthesis for follow-up imaging (such as diagnostic mammography, ultrasound, or MRI); its middle 50% of hospitals fall between 4.7% and 8.9% (median 6.6%), with outliers extending up to 78.0%.
Importantly, lower percentages do not always indicate better hospital performance, nor do these two measures represent overall hospital quality. For OP-10, avoiding routine double-contrast CT scans reduces unnecessary radiation exposure, but combined studies are still clinically appropriate for certain diagnoses. For OP-39, a recall rate that is too high can cause unnecessary follow-up imaging and patient anxiety, whereas a recall rate that is too low could mean missed cancers. From these data, we can reasonably conclude that most U.S. hospitals cluster below 10% on both measures, while a small number of facilities exhibit substantially higher rates that may reflect differences in patient populations, clinical protocols, or facility specialization rather than overall hospital quality.

title: Hospital Comparisons
text:

The measures describe different imaging processes and use different clinical contexts. This chart is for exploring reported values—not for ranking hospitals or interpreting the relationship as a measure of quality.

text:
OP-10 and OP-39 reported percentages
Use the hover details to inspect individual facilities. Hospitals missing either score are not shown; missing values are not treated as zero.






OP-10 tracks outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast. OP-39 tracks screening mammograms followed by diagnostic imaging within 45 days. See the CMS dataset for the source records.

title: Mammography
text:
OP-39 — Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates reports the percentage of screening mammograms followed by diagnostic imaging within 45 days. Follow-up may include additional mammography, ultrasound, or MRI.
A recall can be a necessary part of screening, while unnecessary follow-up can add cost and anxiety. The rate alone cannot distinguish appropriate follow-up from avoidable callbacks, and it should not be treated as a stand-alone measure of a hospital’s overall quality.
The charts below use hospitals with an available OP-39 score in the July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025 reporting period.

title: CT Imaging
text:
OP-10 — Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material reports the percentage of a hospital’s outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast. Looking at both sets of images can be clinically appropriate in some situations, so a higher percentage is not, by itself, proof of poor care.
This CMS measure concerns one specific CT practice; it is not a measure of every CT scan or of overall hospital quality. The charts below show hospitals with an available OP-10 score in the July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025 reporting period.
